data.title: Becker's nevus — viva
data.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Becker's nevus** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. Write a short note on Becker's naevus (PYQ).**
- Acquired-appearing (often congenital but noticed around adolescence) unilateral, large, irregular, light- to dark-brown patch with geographic border on shoulder, upper chest, scapula, upper arm, with hypertrichosis (coarse dark hair) appearing later; men 4–6× more (androgen-dependent — increased androgen receptors)
- A smooth-muscle hamartoma component (Becker's naevus = hamartoma of epidermis, melanocytes, smooth muscle, hair)
- Postzygotic ACTB (β-actin) mutations

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Patch becomes darker and thicker after sun exposure/puberty; acneiform lesions within, pseudo-Darier's sign (smooth muscle — transient elevation/piloerection on rubbing); usually single; may be multiple or bilateral

**Q3. What is Becker's naevus syndrome?**
- Becker's naevus with ipsilateral hypoplasia of breast/areola (most common), pectoralis major, limb shortening, scoliosis, spina bifida, supernumerary nipples, lipoatrophy — included in the epidermal naevus syndromes

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Mild acanthosis with elongated flat-bottomed pigmented rete ridges (basal hyperpigmentation), increased melanin with normal or slightly increased melanocytes, increased smooth muscle bundles in the dermis (smooth muscle hamartoma overlap), prominent hair follicles

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Café-au-lait macule (no hair, earlier onset), congenital melanocytic naevus (raised, darker, nested), smooth muscle hamartoma (congenital, pseudo-Darier's), nevus spilus, plexiform neurofibroma, McCune–Albright CALM, PIH, segmental pigmentation

**Q6. Management.**
- Reassurance — benign; no malignant potential
- Cosmetic: Q-switched/picosecond lasers (pigment — variable, recurrence), fractional lasers, long-pulsed alexandrite/diode laser hair removal (addresses hypertrichosis and can lighten pigment); camouflage
- Topical flutamide (anti-androgen) for breast hypoplasia reported; spironolactone for associated hypoplasia (reports)

**Q7. Describe the clinical features in detail.**
- Unilateral, irregular, large (often >10 cm) light-to-dark brown patch with 'geographic' map-like border on shoulder, upper chest or back of adolescent males; hypertrichosis (coarse hair) develops after pigmentation; acne localised to patch; may show perifollicular papules (smooth muscle)

**Q8. Histopathology in detail.**
- Acanthosis with elongated, flat-bottomed rete ridges, basal hyperpigmentation (melanocytes slightly increased), increased hair follicles, and bundles of smooth muscle (smooth-muscle hamartoma overlap) in dermis

**Q9. What is the association with smooth muscle hamartoma?**
- Becker's naevus and congenital smooth muscle hamartoma lie on a spectrum — both show smooth muscle bundles and hypertrichosis; pseudo-Darier sign (transient piloerection/ elevation on rubbing) can occur

**Q10. Explain Becker's naevus syndrome features.**
- Ipsilateral breast hypoplasia (or nipple/ areolar hypoplasia), pectoralis major hypoplasia, supernumerary nipples, limb shortening, scoliosis, spina bifida, lipoatrophy — examine chest wall and spine

**Q11. Is there a malignancy risk?**
- No significant malignant potential; rare reports of melanoma within (coincidental); counsel benign nature

**Q12. Differential diagnosis in detail.**
- Café-au-lait macule (no hair, from birth, uniform), congenital melanocytic naevus (present at birth, darker, raised, hairy), nevus spilus (speckles), plexiform neurofibroma (soft mass), McCune–Albright CALM, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, tinea versicolor

**Q13. What is the genetic basis?**
- Post-zygotic activating mutations in ACTB (β-actin) in a mosaic patch — explaining hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis and smooth-muscle hamartoma features (androgen-sensitive)

**Q14. Why is it more visible after puberty?**
- Increased androgen receptor expression in the lesion — hair and pigmentation become prominent under pubertal androgens; men more affected; acne may be localised to the lesion

**Q15. Lasers in Becker's naevus.**
- Long-pulsed alexandrite/diode/Nd:YAG lasers for hair; Q-switched/picosecond Nd:YAG or ruby for pigment (frequent recurrence), fractional 1550 nm; patch test spot first; topical flutamide (anti-androgen) reported

## Quick spotter facts
- Unilateral brown patch with coarse hair on the shoulder of a young man — Becker's naevus
- Ipsilateral breast hypoplasia — Becker's naevus syndrome

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Becker's naevus). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
